one_liner: OpenMP-task parallel merge sort for int arrays with AVX2/AVX-512 bitonic base cases; claims about 2.2x over tbb::parallel_sort.
what_it_does: Sorts a plain int array ascending using all OpenMP threads. The API is a single C-style call, ptms::sort_int(int* a, int* buf, int n, int threads = 0), where the caller supplies a scratch buffer of at least n ints that must not alias a; it is not an iterator/comparator interface and handles only 32-bit int keys. ptms::simd_level() reports which kernel set (AVX-512, AVX2 or scalar) was compiled in.
how_it_is_fast: The array is cut into P equal chunks (one OpenMP task each); each chunk's two halves are sorted by a sequential top-down merge sort that ping-pongs between the array and the scratch buffer to avoid copy-back, with optimal sorting networks (branchless min/max compare-exchange) for 4-7 elements and in-register bitonic sorting networks for 8 and 16 elements (AVX2 permutevar8x32 + min/max + blend; AVX-512 permutexvar + mask_blend). The resulting 2P runs are merged pairwise level by level as OpenMP tasks (a binary merge tree, not a loser/tournament tree despite the name), and each pairwise merge is itself parallelised by binary splitting (median of the larger run plus lower_bound in the other) down to 2048 elements or depth 5, so the final merge is not a serial bottleneck. Leaf merges use a branchless select loop.
when_to_use: Sorting millions of 32-bit ints on a multicore x86-64 machine where the code already links OpenMP and an extra n-int scratch buffer is affordable.
Throughput-oriented batch sorts of uniform random int data at full core count, the only workload the author measured (4M ints, 16 threads, Ryzen 9 6900HX).
As a compact (one ~480-line .cpp plus header) reference for combining OpenMP tasks, parallel binary-split merging and AVX2/AVX-512 bitonic base cases.
when_not_to_use: Any key type other than int (no 64-bit, float, key-value, struct or custom-comparator support); use IPS4o, vqsort or x86-simd-sort.
Memory-constrained code: it needs a second n-int buffer, whereas IPS4o sorts in place.

Production code that needs trust in the numbers: the repo appeared on 2026-10-10 (10 commits, 0 stars, no issues or releases), the std::sort and tbb::parallel_sort rows have no public harness, and there is no head-to-head against IPS4o or other parallel sorts.
Arrays above 2^31-1 elements (n is int), or calls made from inside an existing OpenMP parallel region, where the nested region runs on one thread by default.
Plain MSVC cl.exe builds: README says MSVC lacks #pragma omp taskgroup, so Windows needs clang-cl or MinGW GCC (the CI uses MinGW).

integration.form: static lib (CMake target ptms_lib built from src/ptms.cpp); also usable as a source-drop of src/ptms.cpp, src/ptms_detail.h and include/ptms.h
integration.dependencies: OpenMP 4.5+ (tasks and taskgroup); CMake 3.15+ for the provided build
integration.min_toolchain: C++17; GCC 9+, Clang 10+, or clang-cl from Visual Studio 2019+ (README); CI builds with ubuntu-latest g++, MSYS2 MinGW-w64 GCC and macOS Apple Clang + libomp
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AVX2 or AVX-512F for the SIMD base cases; scalar fallback (-DSIMD=SCALAR) on other targets, CI-tested on macOS arm64 in scalar mode only
integration.thread_safety: Header: not thread-safe, do not call concurrently on overlapping data; each call opens its own OpenMP parallel region with P threads

gotchas: sort_int silently returns without sorting when a or buf is null or buf == a; there is no error code or exception.

The default CMake mode (SIMD=AUTO) adds -march=native globally, so binaries are not portable; when the compiler rejects -march=native it falls back to -mavx2, which breaks non-x86 builds unless -DSIMD=SCALAR is passed (the macOS CI job does this).

Harness flaws behind the README numbers: benchmark/benchmark.cpp times only PTMS (no std::sort or TBB code, no TBB link), and it times the internal ptms::detail::sort_body inside an already-open parallel region rather than the public sort_int; its self-test checks copies of the 4-7 sorting networks, not the library's own or SIMD kernels (outputs are still compared with std::sort at four of the 600 timed runs). The 'cache-resident' label does not hold: 16 MB input plus 16 MB scratch against a 16 MB L3.

No correctness bug found: I checked the 4-7 networks exhaustively with the 0-1 principle, emulated the AVX2 and AVX-512 bitonic sort/merge permutation and blend masks (exhaustive 0-1 inputs for the sorts, 20,000 random merges), and ran a sequential Python port of the whole pipeline for n = 4..199, 1000, 4097 and 10007 with P = 1..16 against sorted(); this is an emulation, not a native build. With 32 runs (16 threads) the merge tree has 5 levels, so every call ends with an extra full-array memcpy from the scratch buffer.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: IPS4o is the like-for-like parallel sibling (in-place, generic types, peer-reviewed benchmarks) and should be the default; vqsort and x86-simd-sort cover single-thread SIMD sorting for more key types. Pick PTMS only if you want a small, MIT, OpenMP-only int32 merge sort to vendor or study and can supply a scratch buffer; no comparison against IPS4o exists.
verified_claims_summary: On a Ryzen 9 6900HX (16 threads, AVX2 build; compiler unstated, CMake defaults to -O3 -march=native), sorting 4M uniform random ints in [-1e6, 1e6] took a median 0.0163 s versus 0.036 s for tbb::parallel_sort (about 2.2x, the like-for-like figure) and 0.300 s for single-thread std::sort (the headline 18.4x). Only the PTMS row comes from public code (median of 600 runs after 400 warm-ups, input recopied outside the timer); the baseline rows and the AVX-512 7500F figure (0.0162 s at 12 threads) have no published harness.
status_note: Brand-new single-author project (10 commits, all on 2026-10-10, 0 stars, CI on Linux, Windows and macOS; LICENSE and CITATION.cff dated 2025), MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor, but unproven: no independent measurement and no public baseline harness.
